activities.title: How fast does gossip spread?
activities.objective: Model how a new block spreads through a peer-to-peer network by gossip.
activities.scenario: Each node that learns a block tells a number of random peers in the next round (the fanout). Work out how many nodes know it after each round and how many rounds it takes to reach everyone.
steps: In B3 work out the nodes informed after round 1: the smaller of the total (B10) and the nodes informed before, times one plus the fanout (B11). Lock the total and the fanout with dollar signs and fill down to B8 (round 6).
In C2 to C8 work out the share of the network informed: nodes divided by the total.
In B12 count how many rounds were needed to inform at least 99% of nodes by counting the rows below 0.99 with COUNTIF on C2:C8.

checks.label: B3 is round 1
checks.explain: Each informed node tells fanout more nodes.

checks.label: B5 is round 3
checks.hint: Fill down.
checks.explain: Growth by a factor of nine each round, capped at the total.

checks.label: B8 is round 6
checks.hint: Fill down.

checks.label: C8 is the share after round 6
B12 is the rounds needed

cells.A11: Fanout (peers told per node per round)

activities.title: How big does a chain get, and how long to sync?
activities.objective: Estimate the growth of a chain's storage and the time a new node needs to download it.
activities.scenario: A chain produces blocks at a steady pace. A new node must download and verify the whole history. (Teaching numbers, not any specific chain.)
steps: In B7 work out the blocks per day: 86,400 seconds divided by the block time (B2).
In B8 work out the data added per day in megabytes: blocks per day times the average block size in kilobytes (B3) divided by 1,000.
In B9 work out the size after the given number of years (B4) in gigabytes: data per day times 365 times the years divided by 1,000.
In B10 work out the hours needed to download it at the speed in B5 (megabits per second): size in GB times 8,000 divided by the speed and divided by 3,600.
In B11 show Hard for ordinary users if the size is above 500 GB, else Manageable.

checks.label: B7 is blocks per day
checks.explain: Seconds per day over block time.

checks.label: B8 is MB added per day
checks.explain: Blocks times size in kilobytes, over 1,000.

checks.label: B9 is the size in GB
checks.explain: Per day times days, in gigabytes.

checks.label: B10 is the download time
checks.explain: Gigabytes to megabits, then divide by speed and seconds per hour.

checks.label: B11 is the verdict
checks.hint: =IF(B9>500,"Hard for ordinary users","Manageable")

activities.title: How much cheaper is a rollup?
activities.objective: Calculate the cost per transaction when many transactions share one base-layer batch.
activities.scenario: Posting a batch to the base chain costs a fixed amount, however many transactions it holds. The rollup also charges a small fee per transaction. Compare with sending each transaction directly to the base chain. (Teaching figures.)
steps: In B7 work out the base-layer cost per transaction when sent directly: the base cost per transaction (B2).
In B8 work out the share of the batch cost carried by each transaction: batch cost (B3) divided by transactions per batch (B4).
In B9 add the rollup's own fee per transaction (B5).
In B10 work out how many times cheaper the rollup is: B7 divided by B9.
In B11 work out the saving per 1,000 transactions: (B7 minus B9) times 1,000.

checks.label: B7 is the direct cost
checks.hint: Try the formula =B2 here.

checks.label: B8 is the batch share
B9 is the rollup cost per transaction
checks.explain: Batch share plus the rollup's fee.

checks.label: B10 is how many times cheaper
B11 is the saving per 1,000

cells.A2: Base-layer cost of a direct transaction (rupees)
cells.A3: Cost of posting one batch to the base layer (rupees)
cells.A8: Batch cost carried by each transaction

activities.title: How reliable is your RPC setup?
activities.objective: Use redundancy to work out the availability of a service that depends on several providers.
activities.scenario: A dApp can use several node providers. If each is independently available a given share of the time, the app works whenever at least one is up. (Assumes failures are independent, which is optimistic.)
steps: In B6 work out the chance that all providers are down at once: the single-provider downtime (1 minus B2) raised to the number of providers (B3) using POWER.
In B7 work out the availability with all providers: 1 minus B6.
In B8 work out the downtime in minutes per month for one provider: (1 minus B2) times 43,200.
In B9 work out the downtime in minutes per month for the redundant setup: B6 times 43,200.
In B10 show Excellent if the redundant availability is at least 0.9999, else Good.

checks.label: B6 is the chance all are down
checks.hint: =POWER(1-B2,B3)
checks.explain: Each provider fails 1 in 100; all three at once is 1 in a million.

checks.label: B7 is the combined availability
checks.hint: Try the formula =1-B6 here.
checks.explain: The opposite of all being down.

checks.label: B8 is one provider's downtime
B9 is the redundant downtime
B10 is the rating
checks.hint: =IF(B7>=0.9999,"Excellent","Good")
